questions.q: Which mineral is mainly used in making steel, about 10 kg of it being needed to make one tonne of steel?
questions.e: Manganese is also used to make bleaching powder, insecticides and paints.

questions.q: In Jowai and Cherrapunjee in Meghalaya, coal is dug out by family members through long narrow tunnels. This is called ______ mining.
questions.e: In Meghalaya, mineral ownership lies with individuals and communities, and rat-hole mining is done by family members.

questions.q: Which range of hills in the Bastar district of Chhattisgarh produces very high-grade haematite iron ore?
questions.e: Bailadila ore is exported to Japan and South Korea via Visakhapatnam port.

questions.q: The Khetri mines in Rajasthan are famous for which mineral?
questions.e: The Balaghat mines in Madhya Pradesh and the Khetri mines in Rajasthan are important for copper.

questions.q: India has experimental geothermal energy projects in the Parvati valley near Manikarn in Himachal Pradesh and in the ______ valley in Ladakh.
questions.e: Geothermal energy is heat and electricity produced using heat from the interior of the earth.

questions.q: In which year did Sri Lanka emerge as an independent country?
questions.e: After independence in 1948, leaders of the Sinhala community sought to secure dominance over government by virtue of their majority.

questions.q: In 1956, an Act was passed in Sri Lanka to recognise which as its only official language?
questions.e: The Act disregarded Tamil and was one of the majoritarian measures that alienated Sri Lankan Tamils.

questions.q: Which city was chosen as the headquarters of the European Union?
questions.e: Belgium's arrangement for sharing power in Brussels made the city suitable as the headquarters of the EU.

questions.q: Sharing of power among governments at different levels, such as the union, state and local governments, is called ______ division of power.
questions.e: In vertical division, higher and lower levels of government share power.

questions.q: In horizontal power sharing, each organ of government checks the others. This arrangement is called a system of checks and ______.
questions.e: Checks and balances ensure that none of the organs can exercise unlimited power.

questions.q: Between 1970 and 1993, how many times did Belgium amend its constitution to accommodate its language communities?
questions.e: The Belgian leaders amended their constitution four times to work out an arrangement in which everyone could live together.

questions.q: According to the Sri Lankan constitution, the state shall protect and foster which religion?
questions.e: This provision was one of the measures that made Sri Lankan Tamils feel that the constitution denied them equal rights.

questions.q: When two or more political parties come together to form a government, it is called a ______ government.
questions.e: A coalition government is a form of power sharing among political parties.

questions.q: According to NCERT, Sinhala speakers form about what percentage of Sri Lanka's population?
questions.e: Sinhala speakers form about 74 per cent and Tamil speakers about 18 per cent of the population.

questions.q: Tamils in Sri Lanka whose forefathers came from India as plantation workers during the colonial period are called ______ Tamils.
questions.e: Of the 18 per cent Tamil speakers, 13 per cent are Sri Lankan Tamils and the rest are Indian Tamils.

questions.q: Which kind of reason for power sharing holds that it is the very spirit of democracy, and not merely a way of avoiding conflict?
questions.e: Prudential reasons stress better outcomes, while moral reasons treat power sharing as valuable in itself.

questions.q: The Belgian constitution prescribes that the number of Dutch-speaking and French-speaking ministers in the central government shall be ______.
questions.e: Some special laws require the support of the majority of members from each linguistic group, so no single community can make decisions unilaterally.

questions.q: Subjects of national importance such as defence, foreign affairs, banking, communications and currency are included in the ______ List.
questions.e: The Union government alone can make laws on the subjects in the Union List.

questions.q: Subjects of state and local importance such as police, trade, commerce, agriculture and irrigation are included in the ______ List.
questions.e: The state governments alone can make laws on the subjects in the State List.

questions.q: The president of a gram panchayat is called the ______.
questions.e: The gram panchayat is a council of ward members (panch) and a president (sarpanch).

questions.q: Federations like the USA, Switzerland and Australia, formed when independent states come together to form a bigger unit, are called ______ federations.
questions.e: In coming-together federations, all the constituent states usually have equal power and are strong vis-a-vis the federal government.

questions.q: In a municipal corporation, the political head is called the ______.
questions.e: The municipal chairperson is the political head of a municipality; in a municipal corporation the officer is called the mayor.

questions.q: All the panchayat samitis or mandals in a district together constitute the ______.
questions.e: Most members of the zilla parishad are elected; MPs and MLAs of the district and some officials are also members.

questions.q: Which independent institution has been created in each state to conduct panchayat and municipal elections?
questions.e: The 1992 amendment provided for a State Election Commission in each state.

questions.q: All the voters in a village are members of the ______, which supervises the work of the gram panchayat and must meet at least twice or thrice a year.
questions.e: The gram sabha approves the annual budget of the gram panchayat and reviews its performance.

questions.q: How many languages are included in the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution as Scheduled Languages?
questions.e: Besides Hindi, 21 other languages are recognised as Scheduled Languages.

questions.q: In which year did Belgium shift from a unitary to a federal form of government?
questions.e: In 1993 the regional governments of Belgium were given constitutional powers that were no longer dependent on the central government.

questions.q: Areas like Chandigarh and Lakshadweep, which are too small to become independent states and could not be merged with existing ones, are called ______.
questions.e: Union Territories do not have the powers of a state; the central government has special powers in running them.

questions.q: The fundamental provisions of India's federal structure cannot be changed by the Union government alone.
p: (a) With what majority must a change be passed in both Houses of Parliament?
Two-thirds|Two thirds|2/3|Two-third
(b) At least what fraction of the total states must then ratify the change through their legislatures?
Half|One-half|One half|1/2
(c) Which institution acts as an umpire if disputes arise between different levels of government?
Supreme Court|Courts|Judiciary|Highest court
questions.e: An amendment needs a two-thirds majority in both Houses and ratification by at least half of the states; the courts settle disputes over the division of powers.

questions.q: A political party has three components: the leaders, the active members and the ______.
questions.e: Followers support the party; active members and leaders run it.

questions.q: A group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power in the government is called a ______.
questions.e: Political parties agree on some policies and programmes for society with a view to promoting the collective good.

questions.q: Which political party was founded in 1885?
questions.e: The Indian National Congress, one of the oldest parties in the world, played a dominant role in Indian politics after independence.

questions.q: The Bahujan Samaj Party was formed in 1984 under the leadership of ______.
questions.e: The BSP seeks to represent and secure power for the bahujan samaj, which includes Dalits, Adivasis, OBCs and religious minorities.

questions.q: In which year was the Bharatiya Janata Party founded?
questions.e: The BJP was founded in 1980 by reviving the Bharatiya Jana Sangh, formed in 1951 by Syama Prasad Mukherjee.

questions.q: When several parties in a multiparty system join hands to contest elections and win power, the grouping is called an alliance or a ______.
questions.e: Examples given by NCERT include the NDA, the UPA and the Left Front.

questions.q: A party that secures at least six per cent of the votes in a State Legislative Assembly election and wins at least two seats is recognised as a ______ party.
questions.e: The Election Commission lays down these criteria; state parties are commonly called regional parties.

questions.q: In which year was the Communist Party of India (Marxist) founded?
questions.e: The CPI(M) was founded in 1964; the Communist Party of India dates from 1925.

questions.q: The Supreme Court has made it mandatory for every candidate who contests elections to file an ______ giving details of property and criminal cases.
questions.e: This information is made public so that voters can make an informed choice.

questions.q: A person who is strongly committed to a party, group or faction is called a ______.
questions.e: Partisanship is marked by a tendency to take a side and an inability to take a balanced view.

questions.q: The Election Commission has made it necessary for political parties to hold organisational elections and file their ______ returns.
questions.e: This is one of the steps taken to reform political parties.

questions.q: When top positions in a party are always controlled by members of one family, the challenge is called ______ succession.
questions.e: Dynastic succession is unfair to other members and bad for democracy, since people without adequate experience may reach positions of power.

questions.q: The number of children who die before the age of one year as a proportion of 1000 live children born in that year is called the ______.
questions.e: The infant mortality rate is an important indicator of health facilities.

questions.q: The proportion of the literate population in the 7 years and above age group is called the ______.
questions.e: The literacy rate is one of the indicators used to compare levels of education.

questions.q: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the needs of future generations is called ______ development.
questions.e: Sustainability of development is essential because many resources, like groundwater and crude oil, can be exhausted.

questions.q: The total number of children of age group 14 and 15 years attending school as a percentage of the total number of children of the same age group is called the ______.
questions.e: The net attendance ratio is used to compare how many children in an age group actually attend school.

questions.q: Which index, calculated by dividing a person's weight in kg by the square of the height in metres, is used to find out whether adults are undernourished?
questions.e: A BMI below 18.5 indicates that a person is undernourished; above 25 indicates overweight.

questions.q: Which international organisation uses per capita income in its World Development Report to classify countries?
questions.e: The World Development Report classifies countries as rich or low-income on the basis of per capita income.

questions.q: Equal treatment, freedom, security and respect for others are ______ goals of development.
questions.e: People seek not only more income but also things that cannot be easily measured in money.

questions.q: The average expected length of life of a person at the time of birth is called ______.
questions.e: Life expectancy at birth is one of the indicators in the Human Development Report.

questions.q: Which of the following is a non-material goal of development?
questions.e: Equal treatment cannot be bought with money; the others are material goals.

questions.q: Besides life expectancy and education, which indicator does the Human Development Index use?
questions.a: Per capita income|Income|Gross national income per capita|GNI per capita
questions.e: The HDI combines health, education and per capita income to compare countries.

questions.q: In the Human Development Report, the average number of years of education received by people aged 25 and above is called mean years of ______.
questions.e: Mean years of schooling and expected years of schooling are the education indicators in the report.

questions.q: Things like security, pollution-free environment and protection from infectious diseases are cheaper to provide collectively. Such facilities are called ______ facilities.
questions.e: Money in hand cannot buy all the goods and services needed to live well; some are best provided collectively.

questions.t: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.q: Activities that produce goods by exploiting natural resources, such as agriculture, dairy, fishing and forestry, belong to the ______ sector.
questions.e: The primary sector is also called the agriculture and related sector.

questions.t: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.q: The sector in which natural products are changed into other forms through manufacturing is the ______ sector.
questions.e: The secondary sector is also called the industrial sector, since it is associated with different kinds of industries.

questions.t: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.q: Activities that do not produce a good themselves but aid production, such as transport, banking and trade, belong to the tertiary or ______ sector.
questions.e: The tertiary sector generates services rather than goods.

questions.t: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.q: The value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year is called its ______.
questions.e: GDP shows how big the economy is; in India it is measured by a central government ministry.

questions.t: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.q: A situation in which people are working less than their potential, for example when more people than needed work on a family farm, is called ______.
questions.e: In such a case each worker is working, but no one is fully employed.

questions.t: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.q: Small and scattered units, largely outside the control of the government, where jobs are low-paid and often not regular, form the ______ sector.
questions.e: Unorganised sector workers have no provision for overtime, paid leave or holidays, and can be asked to leave without reason.

questions.t: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.q: Tata Iron and Steel Company Limited and Reliance Industries Limited are owned by private individuals. They are in the ______ sector.
questions.e: Activities in the private sector are guided by the motive to earn profits.

questions.t: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.q: Under MGNREGA, if the government fails in its duty to provide employment, it must give ______ to the people.
questions.e: MGNREGA makes the right to work a legal entitlement for rural households.

questions.t: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.q: According to NCERT, which sector continues to be the largest employer in India, with more than half of the workers?
questions.e: Although the tertiary sector produces the largest share of GDP, most workers are still in the primary sector, mainly agriculture.

questions.t: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.q: Organised sector workers get paid leave, payment during holidays, gratuity and a ______ fund, to which the employer also contributes.
questions.e: These benefits make jobs in the organised sector more secure than those in the unorganised sector.

questions.t: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.q: Only the value of final goods and services is counted in GDP. This is done to avoid ______ counting.
questions.e: The value of final goods already includes the value of all the intermediate goods used in making them.

questions.t: Economics: Sectors of the Indian Economy
questions.q: A farmer sells wheat to a flour mill for ₹8 per kg. The mill grinds it and sells the flour to a biscuit company for ₹10 per kg. Using the flour and other things, the company makes four packets of biscuits and sells them to consumers for ₹60.
p: (a) Which of these is the final good?
Biscuits|Biscuit
(b) What value should be counted in GDP for this chain of production?
(c) How much value does the flour mill add per kg?
questions.e: Only the final good, biscuits worth ₹60, is counted; the mill adds ₹10 - ₹8 = ₹2 per kg.

questions.q: The exchange of goods for goods without the use of money is called the ______ system.
questions.e: Barter needs a double coincidence of wants, which money eliminates.

questions.q: A paper instructing the bank to pay a specific amount from a person's account to the person in whose name it has been issued is called a ______.
questions.e: Cheques allow payments to be made directly from demand deposits without cash.

questions.q: In a barter system, both parties must want to sell what the other wishes to buy. This is called a double ______ of wants.
questions.e: Money acts as a medium of exchange and removes the need for a double coincidence of wants.

questions.q: Which institution issues currency notes on behalf of the central government in India?
questions.e: According to Indian law, no other individual or organisation is allowed to issue currency.

questions.q: The rupee is widely accepted as a medium of exchange because the law legalises its use. It is therefore called legal ______.
questions.e: No individual in India can legally refuse a payment made in rupees.

questions.q: Interest rate, collateral, documentation requirement and mode of repayment together make up the ______ of credit.
questions.e: Terms of credit vary depending on the nature of the lender and the borrower.

questions.q: According to NCERT, banks in India these days hold about what percentage of their deposits as cash?
questions.e: Banks keep about 15 per cent as cash to pay depositors who may come to withdraw, and use most of the rest to extend loans.

questions.q: Loans from banks and cooperatives are called ______ sector loans.
questions.e: Moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives and friends make up the informal sector.

questions.q: Self-Help Groups aim to organise the rural poor, in particular ______, into small groups that pool their savings.
questions.e: A typical SHG has 15 to 20 members, usually belonging to one neighbourhood, who meet and save regularly.

questions.q: After a year or two of regular savings, a Self-Help Group becomes eligible to take a loan from a ______.
questions.e: The loan is sanctioned in the name of the group and is meant to create self-employment opportunities for members.

questions.q: A farmer needs ₹10,000 for 6 months. A moneylender charges simple interest of 3% per month, while a bank charges simple interest of 12% per year.
p: (a) What is the moneylender's interest for one month?
(b) What is the moneylender's total interest for 6 months?
(c) What is the bank's interest for 6 months?
(d) Which of the two is a formal source of credit?
Bank|The bank
questions.e: 3% of ₹10,000 is ₹300 a month, or ₹1,800 for 6 months; at 12% a year the bank charges ₹600 for half a year. Banks are formal lenders.

questions.t: History: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: The ancient trade routes that linked China with the West and other parts of Asia are known as the ______ routes.
questions.e: The name comes from the Chinese silk carried westwards along them; they also carried pottery, spices, textiles, people, ideas and religions.

questions.t: History: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: Which food crop, brought to Europe from the Americas, became so important to poor people in Ireland that its failure in the mid-1840s caused a famine?
questions.e: When disease destroyed the potato crop in the mid-1840s, hundreds of thousands of people in Ireland died of starvation.

questions.t: History: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: Who set up the first assembly line to mass-produce cars, making the T-model?
questions.e: Henry Ford's assembly line in Detroit cut the time and cost of making a car, and mass production became a feature of the US economy.

questions.t: History: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: Indian workers taken abroad on a contract to work for an employer for a fixed number of years were called ______ labourers.
questions.e: An indenture was a bond under which the worker agreed to work for the employer for a set time, usually on plantations, in mines or on construction projects.

questions.t: History: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: Which cattle disease spread through Africa in the 1890s, killing about 90 per cent of the cattle?
questions.e: Rinderpest arrived with infected cattle imported from British Asia; the loss of cattle forced Africans to work for wages for the colonial powers.

questions.t: History: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: Which disease, carried by the Spanish conquerors, killed large numbers of the original inhabitants of America in the sixteenth century, as they had no immunity to it?
questions.e: Germs such as those of smallpox were a more powerful weapon of the conquerors than guns.

questions.t: History: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: The British laws that restricted the import of corn, and were later abolished, were called the ______ Laws.
questions.e: Industrialists and town dwellers wanted cheaper food, so the Corn Laws were abolished and cheap food was imported into Britain.

questions.t: History: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: In which year did the Great Depression begin?
questions.e: The Great Depression began around 1929 and lasted till the mid-1930s, with large falls in production, employment, incomes and trade.

questions.t: History: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: Which nineteenth-century development allowed meat to be carried from Australia, America and New Zealand to Europe without spoiling?
questions.e: Animals were slaughtered at the starting point and carried as frozen meat in refrigerated ships, which made meat cheaper in Europe.

questions.t: History: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: The Bretton Woods conference of July 1944 set up the International Monetary Fund and which other institution?
questions.a: World Bank|the World Bank|IBRD|International Bank for Reconstruction and Development
questions.e: The IMF was to deal with external surpluses and deficits of member nations, and the World Bank (IBRD) was to finance post-war reconstruction.

questions.t: History: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: Under the Bretton Woods system, national currencies were pegged to the US dollar, and the dollar was anchored to gold at how many dollars per ounce?
questions.e: This fixed exchange rate system was the basis of the post-war international monetary order.

questions.t: History: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: Hosay, a carnival in Trinidad in which workers of all races and religions join, grew out of which observance taken there by Indian indentured workers?
questions.e: The annual Muharram procession became Hosay, named after Imam Hussain.

questions.t: History: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: Most nineteenth-century Indian indentured workers came from present-day eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, central India and the dry districts of which state?
questions.e: These regions faced declining cottage industries, rising land rents and land cleared for mines and plantations, which pushed poor people to migrate.

questions.t: History: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: In which year was the system of indentured migration from India abolished?
questions.e: Nationalist leaders opposed indenture as a cruel and abusive system, a 'new system of slavery', and it was abolished in 1921.

questions.t: History: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: The First World War was fought between the Allies (Britain, France and Russia, later joined by the US) and which group of powers?
questions.e: The Central Powers were Germany, Austria-Hungary and Ottoman Turkey. The war lasted from 1914 to 1918.

questions.t: History: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: The Great Depression hit Indian agriculture hard.
p: (a) Between 1928 and 1934, by about what percentage did wheat prices in India fall?
(b) To pay their dues, peasants sold their jewellery and precious metals. Which precious metal did India export in large amounts during the Depression?
gold
questions.e: As international prices crashed, prices in India also plunged: wheat prices fell by 50 per cent, but the colonial government refused to reduce revenue demands. India became an exporter of precious metals, notably gold.

questions.t: History: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: In the nineteenth century, Indian traders and moneylenders also went abroad.
p: (a) Indian traders and moneylenders followed European colonisers into which continent?
Africa
(b) The Shikaripuri shroffs and the Nattukottai ______ were bankers and traders who financed export agriculture in Central and Southeast Asia.
Chettiars|Chettiar
questions.e: Indian traders and moneylenders followed European colonisers into Africa, and groups such as the Shikaripuri shroffs and Nattukottai Chettiars financed export agriculture in Asia.

questions.q: About how much of the earth's surface is covered with water?
questions.e: About three-fourths of the earth's surface is water, but only a small part of it is fresh water that can be used.

questions.q: Jawaharlal Nehru proudly called dams the '______ of modern India'.
questions.e: He believed dams would integrate development of agriculture and the village economy with rapid industrialisation.

questions.q: Collecting and storing rainwater for later use is called rainwater ______.
questions.e: Rooftop rainwater harvesting is common in places such as Rajasthan, Shillong and Tamil Nadu.

questions.q: A river project used for more than one purpose, such as irrigation, electricity, flood control and water supply, is called a ______ river project.
questions.e: Multi-purpose river projects integrate many uses of water from one dam and reservoir.

questions.q: On which river is the Hirakud dam built?
questions.e: The Hirakud project in the Mahanadi basin combines conservation of water with flood control.

questions.q: On which river is the Sardar Sarovar dam built?
questions.e: The Sardar Sarovar dam on the Narmada in Gujarat is one of the largest water resource projects in India.

questions.q: In Bikaner, Phalodi and Barmer in Rajasthan, houses traditionally had underground tanks for storing drinking water. What are these tanks called?
questions.e: Tankas, linked to the sloping roofs by pipes, stored rainwater that lasted into the summer; some houses built rooms next to them to stay cool.

questions.q: In the hilly regions of the western Himalayas, people built diversion channels called 'guls' or '______' for agriculture.
questions.e: Guls or kuls carried water from streams to the fields.

questions.q: In Meghalaya, a 200-year-old system of tapping stream and spring water using bamboo pipes is used for ______ irrigation.
questions.e: About 18-20 litres of water enter the bamboo pipe system, which carries it hundreds of metres and finally drips 20-80 drops a minute at the plant.

questions.q: Which is the first state in India to make rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory for all houses?
questions.e: Tamil Nadu made it compulsory for all houses across the state, with legal provisions to punish defaulters.

questions.q: The Narmada Bachao Andolan later focused on getting full rehabilitation for people ______ by the Sardar Sarovar project.
questions.e: The movement first raised environmental issues about trees that would be submerged, and later worked for poor citizens, especially the displaced people (oustees).

questions.q: In western Rajasthan, rooftop rainwater harvesting is declining because plenty of water is now available from which perennial canal?
questions.a: Rajasthan Canal|Indira Gandhi Canal|Indira Gandhi Nahar
questions.e: Water from the perennial Rajasthan Canal has reduced dependence on tankas, though some houses still keep them.

questions.q: In Rajasthan, rainwater stored in tankas is considered the purest form of natural water. What is it commonly called?
questions.e: Palar pani was a reliable source of drinking water when all other sources dried up in summer.

questions.q: Dams built to control ______ have sometimes triggered them, because sediment builds up in the reservoir.
questions.e: Sedimentation reduces the reservoir's capacity, and excessive release of water during heavy rain has caused floods downstream.

questions.q: Multi-purpose river projects were planned after Independence.
p: (a) On which river is the Bhakra Nangal dam built?
Sutlej|Satluj
(b) Besides generating hydel power, what is the main use of its water?
irrigation
questions.e: The Bhakra Nangal project in the Sutlej-Beas river basin is used both for hydel power production and irrigation.

questions.q: In the arid and semi-arid regions of Rajasthan, farmland was turned into rain-fed storage structures that let water stand and moisten the soil.
p: (a) What are such structures in Jaisalmer called?
khadins|khadin
(b) What are such structures called in other parts of Rajasthan?
johads|johad
questions.e: Khadins in Jaisalmer and johads in other parts of Rajasthan are traditional ways of storing rainwater in fields.

questions.q: Making goods in large quantities by processing raw materials into more valuable products is called ______.
questions.e: Manufacturing belongs to the secondary sector; for example, cotton is made into yarn and cloth.

questions.q: Industries owned and run by the government, such as BHEL and SAIL, are ______ sector industries.
questions.e: Industries are classified by ownership into public, private, joint and cooperative sector industries.

questions.q: Industries such as the sugar industry in Maharashtra, run by the producers or suppliers of raw materials, are ______ sector industries.
questions.e: In cooperative sector industries the producers pool their resources and share the profits or losses.

questions.q: Which bauxite-based metal is produced in India's second most important metallurgical industry?
questions.e: Aluminium smelting is the second most important metallurgical industry in India; aluminium is light, resists corrosion and conducts heat well.

questions.q: In which state are most of India's jute mills, mainly along the banks of the Hugli river?
questions.e: The Hugli basin has jute-growing areas, cheap water transport, coal and abundant water, plus Kolkata as a port and banking centre.

questions.q: India is the largest producer of raw jute and jute goods, and second as an exporter. Which country is the largest exporter?
questions.e: India stands at second place as an exporter of jute goods, after Bangladesh.

questions.q: The iron and steel industry is called a ______ industry, because all other industries depend on it for their machinery.
questions.e: Heavy, medium and light industries all depend on iron and steel for their machinery.

questions.q: Which three raw materials are used to make steel, in a ratio of about 4 : 2 : 1?
questions.a: iron ore, coking coal and limestone
questions.e: Iron ore, coking coal and limestone are needed in the ratio of about 4 : 2 : 1, with some manganese to harden the steel.

questions.q: Which industry uses limestone, silica, alumina and gypsum as its raw materials?
questions.e: Cement plants also need coal, electric power and rail transport; cement is essential for construction.

questions.q: In which city was India's first successful cotton textile mill set up in 1854?
questions.e: The cotton textile industry grew in Maharashtra and Gujarat, close to the cotton-growing belt, ports and markets.

questions.q: The first jute mill in India was set up near Kolkata in 1855 at ______.
questions.e: After Partition in 1947 the jute mills stayed in India, but three-fourths of the jute-producing area went to Bangladesh.

questions.q: Which is the only industry in India that is self-reliant and complete in the value chain, from raw material to the highest value-added products?
questions.e: The textile industry covers everything from raw cotton to yarn, cloth and garments, which gives it a unique place in the Indian economy.

questions.q: Thermal pollution of water happens when hot water from factories and ______ power plants is drained into rivers and ponds before cooling.
questions.e: Hot water harms aquatic life; waste from nuclear plants can also cause cancers and birth defects.

questions.q: Which major power company of India has ISO 14001 certification for its environmental management system?
questions.e: NTPC uses modern technology, makes the best use of equipment, reduces waste and plants trees around its plants to protect the environment.

questions.q: Industries are classified by who owns them.
p: (a) Oil India Ltd, run jointly by the state and individuals, is a ______ sector industry.
joint
(b) TISCO, owned and run by individuals, is a ______ sector industry.
private
questions.e: Public sector: owned by the government; private sector: owned by individuals or groups; joint sector: run jointly by the state and individuals; cooperative sector: owned by the producers of raw materials.

questions.q: Industries are also classified by the raw materials they use.
p: (a) Is the sugar industry agro-based or mineral-based?
agro-based|agro based|agro|agro-based industry
(b) Is the cement industry agro-based or mineral-based?
mineral-based|mineral based|mineral|mineral-based industry
questions.e: Agro-based industries use agricultural raw materials such as cotton, jute, sugarcane and oilseeds; mineral-based industries use minerals, as in iron and steel and cement.

questions.t: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
questions.q: A company that owns or controls production in more than one nation is called a ______.
questions.e: MNCs set up offices and factories for production in regions where they can get cheap labour and other resources.

questions.t: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
questions.q: Money spent to buy assets such as land, buildings, machines and other equipment is called ______.
questions.e: Investment made by MNCs is called foreign investment.

questions.t: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
questions.q: A tax on imports is an example of a trade ______.
questions.e: Governments can use trade barriers to increase or decrease foreign trade and to decide what kinds of goods come into the country.

questions.t: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
questions.q: The rapid integration or interconnection between countries is called ______.
questions.e: More and more goods, services, investments and technology move between countries.

questions.t: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
questions.q: Removing barriers or restrictions set by the government, for example on foreign trade, is called ______.
questions.e: In 1991 the Government of India removed barriers on foreign trade and foreign investment to a large extent.

questions.t: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
questions.q: Which international organisation's aim is to liberalise international trade, and which lays down rules about it?
questions.e: The WTO was started at the initiative of developed countries; about 164 countries are its members.

questions.t: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
questions.q: In which year did the Government of India remove barriers on foreign trade and foreign investment to a large extent?
questions.e: After this, goods could be imported and exported easily, and foreign companies could set up factories and offices in India.

questions.t: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
questions.q: Industrial zones set up by the government, with world-class facilities, to attract foreign companies to invest are called ______.
questions.e: Companies that set up production units in SEZs do not have to pay taxes for an initial period of five years.

questions.t: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
questions.q: What has been the major factor stimulating globalisation?
questions.e: Faster, cheaper transport and the rapid spread of information and communication technology made it possible to organise production across countries.

questions.t: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
questions.q: Cargill Foods, a large American MNC, bought over which small Indian company to become the largest producer of edible oil in India?
questions.e: Buying up local companies and then expanding production is a common way for MNCs to spread production.

questions.t: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
questions.q: Ford Motors, an American car maker, came to India in 1995 and set up a large plant near which city?
questions.e: Ford started in collaboration with Mahindra and Mahindra, and later exported cars and components from India.

questions.t: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
questions.q: Chinese toys became popular in Indian markets mainly because they were ______ and had new designs.
questions.e: Buyers had more choice and lower prices, while Indian toy makers faced losses; trade connects markets across countries.

questions.t: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
questions.q: Which of these Indian companies has itself become a multinational: Infosys, Indian Railways or the State Electricity Board?
questions.e: Indian companies such as Tata Motors, Infosys, Ranbaxy, Asian Paints and Sundaram Fasteners have spread their operations worldwide.

questions.t: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
questions.q: Globalisation that creates opportunities for all and makes sure its benefits are better shared is called ______ globalisation.
questions.e: The government can help by protecting workers' rights, supporting small producers and using trade barriers where needed.

questions.t: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
questions.q: MNCs spread their production across countries.
p: (a) MNCs set up production close to markets, where there is skilled and unskilled ______ available at low cost.
labour|labor
(b) Money that MNCs spend to buy assets in another country is called foreign ______.
investment
questions.e: MNCs choose places with markets, cheap labour, other resources and helpful government policies, and invest there to earn profits.

questions.t: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
questions.q: A government can control foreign trade.
p: (a) A tax on imported goods is an example of a trade ______.
barrier
(b) Does removing such restrictions increase or decrease foreign trade?
increase|increases
questions.e: Trade barriers restrict imports; removing them (liberalisation) lets goods move between countries more easily, so foreign trade increases.

questions.q: The phase of large-scale production for international markets, before factories began, when merchants got goods made by peasants in their homes, is called ______.
questions.e: In proto-industrialisation, merchants from the towns gave money to peasants and artisans in the countryside to produce goods for an international market; it was controlled by merchants, not by factories.

questions.q: Who invented the spinning jenny in 1764?
questions.e: With the spinning jenny, one worker could turn a single wheel that set a number of spindles in motion, spinning several threads at once.

questions.q: A paid servant appointed by the East India Company to supervise weavers, collect supplies and examine the quality of cloth was called a ______.
questions.e: Gomasthas were often outsiders with no long-term link to the village; they acted arrogantly and punished weavers for delays in supply, which led to clashes.

questions.q: Cloth from British mills sold in India carried a label in bold letters saying 'Made in ______', so that buyers trusted its quality.
questions.e: The label 'Made in Manchester' was meant to make buyers confident about the quality of the cloth.

questions.q: Factory owners in India employed a person, usually an old and trusted worker, to get new recruits from his village and to help them settle in the city. What was this person called?
questions.e: The jobber became a person with authority and power: he began demanding money and gifts for his favour and controlling the lives of workers.

questions.q: Which mechanical device for weaving, moved by ropes and pulleys, was used by many Indian weavers in the early twentieth century to increase productivity?
questions.e: With the fly shuttle, the horizontal threads are put into the vertical threads quickly. By 1941, over 35 per cent of handlooms in India had fly shuttles.

questions.q: Associations of producers in English towns that trained craftspeople, controlled production, regulated competition and prices, and restricted new people entering the trade were called ______.
questions.e: Because guilds made it hard to set up business in the towns, merchants turned to peasants and artisans in the countryside.

questions.q: During which war did Indian factories grow quickly, because imports of Manchester goods fell and the mills supplied the army?
questions.a: First World War|World War I|WW1|WWI|the First World War|World War 1
questions.e: British mills were busy with war production, so Manchester imports into India declined; Indian mills had a home market and also supplied jute bags, uniforms, tents and boots to the army.

questions.q: Who created the cotton mill, bringing the costly new machines together under one roof and management?
questions.e: With the cotton mill, the production process could be supervised carefully, quality watched and labour regulated, which was hard when production was in the countryside.

questions.q: In the English wool trade, a person who 'staples' or sorts wool according to its fibre is called a ______.
questions.e: In the chain of production a merchant clothier bought wool from a stapler, carried it to spinners, then to weavers, fullers and dyers, and finished it in London.

questions.q: In which year did the first cotton mill in Bombay come up?
questions.e: The first cotton mill in Bombay came up in 1854 and went into production two years later. By 1862 four mills were at work.

questions.q: Which Bengal industrialist, who made his fortune in the China trade, set up six joint-stock companies in the 1830s and 1840s?
questions.e: Dwarkanath Tagore believed that India would develop through westernisation and industrialisation, and invested in shipping, shipbuilding, mining, banking, plantations and insurance.

questions.q: In 1912, J.N. Tata set up the first iron and steel plant in India at which place?
questions.e: The Tata Iron and Steel plant at Jamshedpur was set up in 1912; Bhilai, Durgapur and Rourkela came up after independence.

questions.q: James Watt improved the steam engine produced by which earlier inventor, and patented the new engine in 1781?
questions.e: Watt's industrialist friend Matthew Boulton manufactured the new model.

questions.q: In 1917, who set up the first Indian jute mill in Calcutta?
questions.e: Seth Hukumchand, a Marwari businessman, set up the first Indian jute mill in Calcutta in 1917; earlier jute mills there were European-owned.

questions.q: In which city was the Elgin Mill started in the 1860s?
questions.e: The Elgin Mill was started in Kanpur in the 1860s; the first spinning and weaving mill of Madras began production in 1874.

questions.q: Species found only in a particular area, such as the Andaman teal and the Nicobar pigeon, are called ______ species.
questions.e: Endemic species are found only in some particular areas, usually isolated by natural or geographical barriers. Other examples are the Andaman wild pig and the mithun in Arunachal Pradesh.

questions.q: In which year was Project Tiger launched in India?
questions.e: Project Tiger was launched in 1973 to protect the tiger, whose numbers had fallen to about 1,827 by that year.

questions.q: Which movement in the Himalayas, in which villagers hugged trees to stop them being cut, resisted deforestation in several areas?
questions.e: The Chipko movement successfully resisted deforestation in several areas and showed that community afforestation with indigenous species can be very successful.

questions.q: Which Act, passed in 1972, gave legal protection to many wildlife species and banned hunting of protected species?
questions.a: Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act|Wildlife Protection Act|Indian Wildlife Protection Act|Wildlife (Protection) Act
questions.e: The Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act of 1972 drew up an all-India list of protected species, banned their hunting and gave legal protection to their habitats.

questions.q: The Bishnois of Rajasthan are known for protecting which animal, along with the chinkara, nilgai and peacocks?
questions.e: Herds of blackbuck, chinkara, nilgai and peacocks are an integral part of the community near Bishnoi villages, and nobody harms them.

questions.q: Which category of forest makes up more than half of the total forest land in India and is regarded as the most valuable for conserving forest and wildlife?
questions.e: Reserved forests are more than half of the total forest land; protected forests are almost one-third, and unclassed forests belong to government, private individuals and communities.

questions.q: The Beej Bachao Andolan, which showed that diversified crops can be grown without synthetic chemicals, began in which area of Uttarakhand?
questions.e: Farmers of the Beej Bachao Andolan in Tehri and Navdanya have shown that diversified crop production without synthetic chemicals is possible and economically viable.

questions.q: The Asiatic cheetah and the pink-headed duck belong to which IUCN category of species?
questions.e: Extinct species are not found after searches of the areas where they might occur; the Asiatic cheetah was declared extinct in India in 1952.

questions.q: In which state is the Sundarbans tiger reserve?
questions.e: Other tiger reserves include Corbett (Uttarakhand), Bandhavgarh (Madhya Pradesh), Sariska (Rajasthan), Manas (Assam) and Periyar (Kerala).

questions.q: Which state passed the first resolution for Joint Forest Management, in 1988?
questions.e: Joint Forest Management involves local communities in managing and restoring degraded forests; members get benefits such as non-timber forest produce and a share in timber.

questions.q: Which state has the largest area under permanent forests in India?
questions.e: Permanent forests make up 75 per cent of Madhya Pradesh's total forest area.

questions.q: Taxol, a compound used to treat some cancers, is extracted from which Himalayan tree?
questions.e: Taxol from the bark, needles, twigs and roots of the Himalayan yew is used against some cancers; over-exploitation has put the tree under great pressure.

questions.q: The blue sheep, the Asiatic elephant and the Gangetic dolphin belong to which IUCN category of species?
questions.e: Vulnerable species have numbers that have declined to levels from which they are likely to become endangered soon if the negative factors continue.

questions.q: The Mundas and Santhals of Chota Nagpur worship the mahua and which other tree during weddings?
questions.e: Many tribal communities worship trees and protect them in sacred groves; the Oraons and Mundas worship the tamarind and mango during weddings.

questions.q: In which district of Rajasthan did the people of five villages declare 1,200 hectares of forest as the Bhairodev Dakav 'Sonchuri', with their own rules banning hunting?
questions.e: The Sonchuri villagers made their own rules and regulations, did not allow hunting, and protected the wildlife against outside encroachments.

questions.q: India has nearly what percentage of the total number of species in the world?
questions.e: India is one of the world's richest countries in biological diversity, with nearly 8 per cent of the world's species (estimated at 1.6 million).

questions.q: The Golden Quadrilateral super highways link Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and which other city?
questions.e: The Golden Quadrilateral is a six-lane super highway project to reduce the time and distance between India's mega cities.

questions.q: The first train in India ran in 1853 from Mumbai to which place?
questions.e: The first train covered a distance of 34 km between Mumbai and Thane.

questions.q: When the value of a country's exports is more than the value of its imports, its balance of trade is called ______.
questions.e: If imports are more than exports, the balance of trade is unfavourable.

questions.q: Roads that link a state capital with the district headquarters are called ______ highways.
questions.e: State highways are built and maintained by the State Public Works Department; national highways link the extreme parts of the country.

questions.q: Which port was developed soon after independence as a major port on the Gujarat coast, to ease the pressure on Mumbai port?
questions.e: Kandla, now called Deendayal Port, is a tidal port; it handles exports and imports of the grain and industrial belts across Gujarat, Rajasthan, Punjab and nearby states.

questions.q: Which is the biggest port of India, with a spacious, natural and well-sheltered harbour?
questions.e: Jawaharlal Nehru port was planned to ease the pressure on Mumbai port and to serve as a hub port for the region.

questions.q: The North-South corridor of super highways links Srinagar with which place?
questions.e: The North-South corridor links Srinagar (Jammu and Kashmir) and Kanyakumari (Tamil Nadu).

questions.q: The East-West corridor of super highways connects Silchar in Assam with which place in Gujarat?
questions.e: The main aim of the super highways is to reduce the time and distance between the mega cities of India.

questions.q: Which government scheme has special provisions so that every village is linked to a major town by an all-season motorable road?
questions.a: Pradhan Mantri Grameen Sadak Yojana|PMGSY|Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana
questions.e: Rural roads link rural areas and villages with towns; the scheme received special impetus under the Pradhan Mantri Grameen Sadak Yojana.

questions.q: National highways are laid and maintained by which body?
questions.e: National highways are primary road systems laid and maintained by the Central Public Works Department (CPWD); many major national highways run north-south and east-west.

questions.q: In which year was the Border Roads Organisation set up to build and maintain roads in the border areas of the country?
questions.e: The Border Roads Organisation, a government of India undertaking set up in 1960, built roads of strategic importance in the northern and north-eastern border areas.

questions.q: The HVJ gas pipeline links Hazira in Gujarat with Vijaipur in Madhya Pradesh and which place in Uttar Pradesh?
questions.e: The Hazira-Vijaipur-Jagdishpur pipeline has branches to Kota in Rajasthan, Shahjahanpur and Babrala in Uttar Pradesh, and other places.

questions.q: Which port in Goa is the premier iron ore exporting port of India?
questions.e: Marmagao port accounts for about fifty per cent of India's iron ore exports.

questions.q: Which is one of the oldest artificial ports of India, second only to Mumbai in volume of trade and cargo?
questions.e: Chennai port on the east coast is one of the oldest artificial ports of the country.

questions.q: Which is the deepest landlocked and well-protected port of India, originally built as an outlet for iron ore exports?
questions.e: Visakhapatnam port in Andhra Pradesh was originally conceived as an outlet for iron ore exports.

questions.q: National Waterway No. 1 runs on the Ganga between Allahabad (Prayagraj) and which place, a distance of 1,620 km?
questions.e: National Waterway No. 2 is the Brahmaputra between Sadiya and Dhubri (891 km), and No. 3 is the West Coast Canal in Kerala.

questions.q: A system in which all work inside the home is done by the women of the family, or organised by them through domestic helpers, is called the sexual division of ______.
questions.e: The sexual division of labour is based on the belief that women's main job is housework and bringing up children, although women also do paid work outside the home.

questions.q: A woman or a man who believes in equal rights and opportunities for women and men is called a ______.
questions.e: Feminist movements are radical women's movements that aim at equality in personal and family life and public affairs.

questions.q: What fraction of the seats in local government bodies, such as panchayats and municipalities, is reserved for women in India?
questions.e: With seats reserved for women, there are now more than ten lakh elected women representatives in rural and urban local bodies.

questions.q: A state that has no official religion and treats all religions equally, as India does, is called a ______ state.
questions.e: Unlike the status of Buddhism in Sri Lanka or Islam in Pakistan, the Constitution of India does not give a special status to any religion.

questions.q: A system that values men more and gives them power over women is called ______.
questions.e: Literally 'rule by father', patriarchy refers to a system that values men more and gives them power over women.

questions.q: Which Act provides that men and women should be paid equal wages for equal work?
questions.a: Equal Remuneration Act|the Equal Remuneration Act|Equal Remuneration Act 1976
questions.e: Even so, in almost all areas of work, from sports and cinema to factories and fields, women are paid less than men, even when both do the same work.

questions.q: The number of girls per thousand boys in a population is called the child ______ ratio.
questions.e: In some parts of India parents prefer sons and find ways to have the girl child aborted before birth, which has reduced the child sex ratio.

questions.q: Laws that deal with family matters such as marriage, divorce, adoption and inheritance are called ______ laws.
questions.e: In India, family laws are different for followers of different religions, and many feminists have pointed out that they discriminate against women.

questions.q: The belief that people who follow one religion form one community, with the same fundamental interests, and that followers of different religions cannot live as equal citizens, is called ______.
questions.e: Communalism can take many forms in politics, from everyday beliefs and religious prejudice to political mobilisation on religious lines and communal violence.

questions.q: In which group of countries, such as Sweden, Norway and Finland, is the participation of women in public life very high?
questions.e: Women's movements made women's political representation an issue; in the Scandinavian countries women take part in public life on a large scale.

questions.q: Which social reformer from Tamil Nadu, known as Periyar, worked for a society free of caste inequalities?
questions.a: E.V. Ramaswami Naicker|E.V. Ramasami|Ramaswami Naicker|E V Ramasamy|Periyar E.V. Ramasamy|E.V. Ramasamy|Periyar
questions.e: Political leaders and social reformers like Jotiba Phule, Gandhiji, B.R. Ambedkar and Periyar Ramaswami Naicker advocated and worked to establish a society without caste inequalities.

questions.q: The Constitution allows the state to intervene in religious matters to ensure equality within religious communities. Which practice, for example, does it ban?
questions.e: This shows that secularism in India is not just an ideology of some parties but one of the foundations of the country.

questions.q: In the traditional caste system, caste was hereditary, and members of the same caste group were expected to follow the same or a similar ______.
questions.e: Caste groups were endogamous and hereditary, and members of the same caste group were supposed to form a social community that practised the same or similar occupation.

questions.q: When parties choose candidates in elections keeping in mind the caste make-up of the electorate, so as to win votes, caste is being used as a ______ bank.
questions.e: Yet no parliamentary constituency in India has a clear majority of one single caste, so every candidate and party needs to win the confidence of more than one caste.

questions.q: In which year was the Equal Remuneration Act passed in India?
questions.e: The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 provides that equal wages should be paid for equal work.

questions.q: The constitutional amendment of 2023, the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, reserves what fraction of the seats in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies for women?
questions.e: The 106th Amendment, 2023 reserves one-third of the seats for women; the reservation takes effect after the next census and the delimitation that follows it.

questions.q: The most basic outcome of democracy is that it produces a government that is ______ to the citizens and responsive to their needs.
questions.e: Democracy ensures that decision-making is based on norms and procedures, and citizens can check whether decisions were taken through the correct procedures.

questions.q: The right and the means of a citizen to examine the process of decision-making in government is called ______.
questions.e: A citizen who wants to know whether a decision was taken through the correct procedures can find this out; this is missing from many non-democratic governments.

questions.q: Democratic government is ______ government: it may be slow, less efficient and not always very responsive, but it is the people's own government.
questions.e: This is why the support for the idea of democracy is overwhelming all over the world.

questions.q: Democracies regularly hold free and fair ______ to choose their rulers.
questions.e: Democracies have had greater success in setting up regular and free elections and in setting up conditions for open public debate.

questions.q: Looking at the rate of economic growth of countries between 1950 and 2000, which type of government had a slightly higher rate on average?
questions.e: The difference is small, and economic growth also depends on population size, global situation, cooperation from other countries and the country's priorities, so democracy cannot be rejected on this basis.

questions.q: Which law gives citizens the right to ask for information from government offices, making government more transparent?
questions.a: Right to Information Act|RTI Act|RTI|Right to Information
questions.e: The Right to Information Act ensures that citizens can find out what the government is doing; it acts as a watchdog of democracy.

questions.q: Democracy is not just rule by the majority opinion: every citizen should have a chance of being in the ______ at some point of time.
questions.e: If someone is barred from being in the majority because of birth, such as their religion, race or language, the rule ceases to be accommodative for that person or group.

questions.q: Which European country is given as an example of a democracy that successfully negotiated differences among ethnic groups?
questions.e: Belgium has successfully negotiated differences among ethnic populations, which reduces the possibility of tensions becoming explosive or violent.

questions.q: Democratic decisions may take more time because democracy is based on the idea of deliberation and ______.
questions.e: Because it has followed procedures, a decision taken this way may be more acceptable to the people and more effective.

questions.q: In which year was the Right to Information Act passed in India?
questions.e: The Right to Information Act, 2005 lets citizens seek information from public authorities within a fixed time.

questions.q: The fact that people complain about democracy is itself a testimony to the ______ of democracy, because it shows that people have become aware and able to look critically at power.
questions.e: A public expression of dissatisfaction with democracy shows that people have developed awareness and the ability to expect more from those in power.

questions.q: Democracy has strengthened the claims of which disadvantaged groups in India for equal status and equal opportunity?
questions.a: disadvantaged and discriminated castes|castes|lower castes|discriminated castes|Dalits
questions.e: There are still instances of caste-based inequalities and atrocities, but these lack the moral and legal foundations; perhaps this recognition makes ordinary citizens value their democratic rights.

questions.q: Which outcome of democracy is shown by the fact that the long struggles of women have created some sensitivity that respect and equal treatment of women are necessary for a democratic society?
questions.a: dignity of women|dignity|dignity and freedom of the citizen|dignity and freedom
questions.e: Democracy is better than any other form of government in promoting the dignity and freedom of the individual.

questions.q: Even in democracies, a small number of ultra-rich people enjoy a highly disproportionate share of wealth and income. Which outcome are democracies said to be not very successful at?
questions.a: reducing economic inequality|reducing inequality|reducing economic inequalities|economic equality|reducing poverty and inequality
questions.e: The share of income of those at the bottom of society has been declining, and they find it difficult to meet basic needs of life, such as food, clothing, housing, education and health.

questions.q: About how many countries of the world today claim and practise some kind of democratic politics?
questions.a: over a hundred|more than a hundred|100|over 100|more than 100|a hundred
questions.e: They have formal constitutions, they hold elections, they have parties and they guarantee rights of citizens, although they differ in social, economic and cultural achievements.

questions.q: In a democracy, a citizen who wants to know whether a decision was taken through the correct procedures can find this out. This right and means of examining decisions is missing in many ______ governments.
questions.e: Democracy ensures that decision-making is based on norms and procedures; this transparency is one reason a democratic government is accountable to its citizens.
